response.passage: Physics can be confusing, so let's clear up some common doubts about gravity and fluids. First, gravity is a universal force of attraction between all objects with mass, whether they are tiny pebbles or massive planets. It does not stop at the edge of our atmosphere; it continues to pull objects together even in the emptiness of space. When we drop objects in a perfect vacuum, they fall at the exact same rate regardless of their mass, because gravity accelerates all objects equally. Furthermore, mass is the amount of matter in an object, while weight is the force exerted by gravity on that mass; they are distinct physical quantities. When you submerge an object in water, it may feel lighter due to the upward buoyant force, but its actual mass remains completely unchanged. Finally, pressure depends on the area over which a force is applied. A sharp nail exerts much higher pressure than a flat board under the same force because the nail concentrates that force onto a tiny surface area, making it easier to pierce materials.
response.summary: This passage explains that gravity acts on all objects regardless of size or location. It also clarifies the differences between mass and weight, and how pressure relates to surface area.
